Efficient Integer-Only-Inference of Gradient

Boosting Decision Trees on

Low-Power Devices

Majed Alsharari , Son T. Mai , Roger Woods , Fellow, IEEE, and Carlos Reaño , Member, IEEE

There is increasingly interest in developing embedded machine learning hardware as it can offer better performance in terms of privacy, bandwidth efficiency, and scalability. Gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT) represent a strong candidate as they employ less complex logic, but their efficient implementation in field programmable gate array (FPGA) needs to be explored in detail. In this paper, we propose sophisticated quantisation approaches to balance the dual goals of efficiency and performance. In particular, we introduce quantisation-aware training of GBDT for integer-only and binary arithmetic. Results are presented for implementations on a Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC FPGA with the best design using only 170 Look-up Tables and 233 flip-flops at a clock speed of 724 MHz. Implementations focused on network intrusion detection and jet substructure classification for large-scale physics experiments are explored. An order of magnitude less FPGA resources are used whilst offering extremely high throughput rate and maintaining accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/malsharari/QATGBDT.
Index Terms— Gradient-boosted decision trees, embedded AI, field programmable gate array, quantization-aware training, design framework.

MPLEMENTING intelligent systems on small-scale devices employing edge computing is a complex yet promising field. With increasing computational and energy costs of large cloud-based systems, it offers the potential to avoid the need for detailed training and produce better performance in terms of privacy, bandwidth efficiency, and scalability. The approach has been applied in numerous areas including smart healthcare [1] and intrusion detection systems [2]. The shift towards edge computing, however, requires models that are not only precise but also compact and energy-efficient.

In machine learning (ML), traditional methods such as decision trees [3], have exhibited distinct characteristics compared to deep neural networks (DNNs). Despite their superior

performance with image, text, and audio data, however, DNNs are not widely used for tabular data which can form a lot of real-world data, as they compromise either numerical or categorical features or both [4]. Gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) such as XGBoost [5], LightGBM [6], and Catboost [7] models have demonstrated the ability to learn with high accuracy for different data representation [8]. Whilst DNNs typically require extensive computational demands, GBDT models often require less computational power [9], [10], [11], [12]. These characteristics make traditional ML models particularly appealing for resource-limited, edge computing environments.

Much DNN architectural evolution has concentrated on model complexity and computational efficiency, inhibiting its deployment in small profile hardware. For this reason, substantial research effort has focused on minimizing the size of DNN models, aiming to achieve this without significantly compromising accuracy either by network pruning [13], quantisation [14], [15], [16], or more aggressively by binarisation [17]. Within this context, decision tree models, and particularly GBDT, emerge as significant as they usually require less computational cost and memory consumption, thus making them more suitable for embedded system deployment. However, a challenge arises when expanding decision tree models as they demand more memory, leading to a trade-off between latency and computational cost [9], [10], [11], particularly for field programmable gate array (FPGA) implementations.

The strategy of reducing bit-widths for the GBDT model parameters is a natural progression enhancing efficiency [10]; indeed, the post-training quantisation (PTQ) technique [20] is a well established approach for quantising DNN models, shrinking both memory footprint and computational complexity. As depicted in Fig. 1, this method has limitations for GBDT models as reducing bit-width can compromise model effectiveness, shown in a decline in the AUC (Area Under the receiver operating characteristic Curve) metric for smaller integer bit-widths, and for both binary and multiclass classification tasks. It is more noticeable for small GBDT model sizes (Fig. 1a), underscoring the necessity for more sophisticated quantisation methods that effectively balance the dual goals of efficiency and performance. Observations from DNN quantisation highlight the need for quantisation-aware training (QAT) [20] in decision trees as it can build models resilient to bit-width reduction, allowing efficient operation without significant accuracy loss.

In this paper, we introduce a structured approach of integer-only inference specifically for GBDT that adapts certain techniques from the DNN domain but diverges from existing methods, offering fresh insights and strategies for creating effective QAT of GBDT models. The efficiency of employing integer-only inference in GBDT models is initially explored before extending it to Binary GBDT implementations. Our approach aims to achieve performance comparable to floating-point versions, pushing the boundaries of current methodologies. While QAT is well-established within the field of DNNs, its application to GBDTs has not been thoroughly explored. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to investigate and present the unique challenges and necessary innovations involved in applying QAT to GBDTs.

The research contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

• Introduction of a systematic approach for implementing QAT in GBDT with emphasis on efficiency and practicality.

• Demonstration of the feasibility of integer-only inference in GBDT, expanding the scope of traditional application of machine learning techniques.

• Proposing the novel concept of Binary GBDT, aiming to achieve performance on par with floating-point models, thereby offering a groundbreaking perspective in the field.

• Numerous GBDT implementations on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC FPGA with the best design using only 170 look-up tables and 233 flip-flops with a clock speed of 724 MHz. The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section II gives an overview of previous work and then the concept of quantised GBDT is outlined in Section III. Next we describe how to make a model aware of the GBDT quantisation process in Section IV. Later in Section V we present a generative hardware implementation of GBDT. Finally, an evaluation of the performance of our approach is given in Section VI and followed by conclusions in Section VII.

The deployment of ML models on embedded systems introduces significant challenges around constrained processing

power, energy consumption and memory footprint. These constraints are interrelated; a model with substantial size might necessitate the use of external memory, leading to elevated power consumption and delays in fetching of external data [21]; complex processing can result in prolonged mathematical operations, increasing power consumption, particularly when changing ML algorithms in embedded systems. These challenges can restrict their effective deployment.

Numerous research efforts have been directed towards addressing these challenges, with a particular focus on model size compression. Quantisation has been identified as having the best potential and relevant pivotal previous work is summarised in this section. The reader is directed to [22] for an in-depth exploration.

The two principal approaches and algorithms for constructing quantised neural networks (QNNs) are PTQ, which is directly applicable to pre-trained models, and QAT, which requires retraining with labelled data [21]. Although quantisation algorithms generally yield comparable performance at higher bit-widths, PTQ struggles to maintain effectiveness at lower precision. K-means quantisation [21] has been explored using PTQ and QAT and shows that it can substantially improve compression rates when combined with pruning.

Another non-linear method called incremental network quantisation (INQ) [23] employs group quantisation for specific weights and retrains the network to mitigate accuracy degradation. Linear quantisation, conversely, rounds floating-point values to their nearest quantised integers after range clipping and scaling. Affine mapping [14] employs scaling and offsetting to map integers to real values. The approach is later enhanced in [16] for integer-only data types, setting the foundation for the methodologies proposed here. To achieve more efficient FPGA acceleration of QNNs, codesign approaches, such as FINN-R [24] and hls4ml [25], have been introduced to efficiently map quantised networks onto the hardware fabric.

Binarisation in neural networks simplifies network parameters to just two potential values, a method leading to the development of binarised neural networks (BNNs). BinaryConnect [26] pioneered this approach by utilising binarised weights during both the forward pass and back-propagation, employing deterministic or stochastic methods for binarisation during DNN model training. BinaryNet [27] expanded this concept to include both weights and activations within its binarisation framework, successfully preserving state-of-theart accuracy levels. Addressing the needs of larger DNN models, XNOR-Net [17] introduced a more refined binarisation technique, leveraging a scaled sign function to facilitate convolution operations via XNOR and bitcounting, thus enhancing hardware efficiency. Both BinaryNet and XNOR-Net implement the ‘straight-through estimation’ strategy [28] to navigate the challenge of zero derivative in the sign function during the back-propagation of binarised weights.

To optimise BNN deployment on FPGAs, co-design methodologies such as FINN [29] and hls4ml have been developed, enabling an efficient translation of BNNs onto hardware platforms. To achieve higher parallelisation, Murovic et al. [30] hard-wired the weights and arithmetic of BNN into the circuitry of FPGA fabric and achieved a completely combinational logic design. Look-up table (LUT)-based implementations target low-latency applications for enhancing the performance and efficiency of BNNs in hardware-constrained environments. Sophisticated approaches like LUTNet [31], LogicNets [32], Logic-shrinkage [33], NullaNet-Tiny [34], and PolyLUT [35] have emerged as further advancement in FPGA implementation. Mostly, these methods specifically rely on increasing network sparsity, reducing network connections or neurons, since the number of LUTs scale-up noticeably with the number of inputs. However, this leads to a degradation of accuracy.

subsection: C. Hardware Deployment of GBDT Model
text:
Compared to other decision trees, GBDT has a unique mechanism based on constructing dependent weak predictors to form a strong one. This dependency implies that the development of a new tree relies on the performance of previous trees during training. Similar to DNNs, compression through the reduction of model trees presents a challenge, a reason to reduce the model size to fit on constrainedmemory devices. HardGBM [36] has explored the possibility of specifically reducing the size of GBDT regression models while maintaining high accuracy through a pruning strategy. Furthermore, HardGBM has proposed an efficient mapping of the compressed regression GBDT model onto FPGA devices.

Similarly, other research work [9], [10], [37] has concentrated on the efficient implementation of GBDT models into FPGA fabric, including co-design implementations. The study in [9] utilises on-chip memory to store tree parameters, adopting 16-bit fixed-point precision for thresholds and leaf nodes to allow for the stacking of more information in each 32-bit block of the FPGA RAM. FAXID [37], another memory-based implementation, proposes a reconfigurable GBDT FPGA accelerator targeting data centres. It retains floating-point precision to preserve high-accuracy results, although is challenged by delays caused by fetching tree parameters from an external memory device. Moreover, hls4ml introduced Conifer by Summer et al. [10], proposed an end-to-end framework for implementing GBDT models on FPGA. Conifer utilises the LUT component to fully implement tree structures on-chip of the FPGA fabric, LUT-based implementations. Though they used fixed-point precision to lower resource usage, precision was limited due to a drop in accuracy.

The work in [38] focused on using quantisation to compress the weights of training samples of boosted decision trees; however, it was not appled to GBDT. Recently, there has been an increased interest in quantised gradients during the training of GBDT. Secureboost+ [39] introduced gradient quantisation as an additional encryption layer for the proposed GBDT federated learning framework. To accelerate the training of

GBDT, BitBoost [40] demonstrated that high accuracy could be achieved with low precision training of gradients. More recently, work in [41] aimed to accelerate the training of GBDT models on specific multi-hardware setups, extending this to cluster-based environments. Importantly, however, these studies did not focus on reducing the model memory size for the inference phase, which enhances their usability in real-world applications where resources are limited.

Many of the aforementioned papers have focused on the efficient implementation/exporting of GBDT into FPGA devices; the reduction in precision (post-quantisation), however, is always countered by a significant reduction in accuracy. Our proposed work focuses on addressing this challenge, thereby improving the efficiency of GBDT hardware implementations.

section: III. QUANTIZED GRADIENT BOOSTED DECISION TREES
text: In this section, we formulate the concept of quantised GBDT model, m. For m, the main variables are the number of estimators (trees), e, the depth of the trees, d, the threshold values, t, and the leaf (score) values, l. We use the applied quantisation representations from [16] where quantised values are represented by q, whereas real values are represented with r, and b is used for the special case of binarised values. The main goal is to effectively transform real values and floatingpoint arithmetic into quantised representations, either integeror binary-only.

section: III. QUANTIZED GRADIENT BOOSTED DECISION TREES
text: Efficient quantisation, as described above, helps minimize the approximation error and ensures that the ensemble model’s predictions are as accurate as possible, even under the constraints of reduced precision. This quantisation typically remains robust against rounding and clipping errors, especially at higher bit-widths (see Fig. 1). Therefore, the efficacy of integer-only GBDT depends on the precision of the quantisation process. An optimal balance between the bit-width and the accuracy of the quantised model is essential for achieving high-performance inference. The subsequent sections will explore the impacts of various quantisation strategies on the model’s accuracy and efficiency.

Whilst post-quantisation of GBDT models produces efficient implementations, it fails to maintain performance for lower bit-widths, as depicted in Fig. 1. Post-quantisation suffers outliers in numerical values of GBDT threshold values as they are data and model training dependent, meaning that small numerical values (i.e. information) are lost when quantised, thus affecting conditional operations. If quantisation can be introduced during training, then the model can be made to be robust against lost information and able to overcome outlier challenges. In this section, we discuss the development of an efficient, pipelined framework, developed to be sensitive to the quantisation process.

Simulated quantisation, also known as fake-quantisation, is a QAT approach that simulates the quantisation effect for quantised inference. For GBDT, unlike DNN, simulated quantisation ensures that, while training the model, it is finetuned with precise floating-point calculations for thresholds and leaf values capturing the intricacies within the data. The training phase uses high precision for calculations, but to simulate a lower bit-width training, a quantisation step is introduced. Parameters are rounded to their nearest integer representation, allowing the model to be prepared for the computational efficient, inference phase. Fig. 2b visualises the quantisation during the training process, showcasing the conversion from floating-point to integer values. This differs from similar approaches in DNN in that the input data is also quantised during training, except for binary input. In addition, each tree is built by forward propagation pass only (i.e. there is not back propagation step), but it depends on previous trees’ loss values. Thus, no more action should be introduced during training, such as the straight-through estimator trick in DNN approaches [28].

To introduce quantisation during tree building, we assume that if previous trees’ threshold and leaf values are quantised, loss values needed for next tree built will force GBDT algorithms to reduce the quantisation effect, such as presented in Fig. 2a. For every new tree built, all previous threshold and leaf values in GBDT model are collected in two separated sets, and one scale value and one zero-point offset are calculated for each set, using Equations (3) or (4). Then, quantisation is applied to update each tree threshold and leave values using first Equation (2) and then Equation (1), such as represented by Fig. 2b. Once the GBDT model is updated, the next tree parameters will be trained, ensuring that the input data is quantised using the same scale value and zero-point offset from previous threshold values, which is important to make the training valid as shown in Equation (5). By doing so, the GBDT model will find best tree splits and score values for the new tree that will reduce the loss value of quantised GBDT trees.

For the inference phase, explained through Fig. 2c, the model operates solely with integers (it could be with binary too). This shift to integer-only streamlines the process, reducing the computational demands whilst still retaining the model’s training accuracy. Similarly, binarisation-aware training follows the same process with only leave values binarised during the training and thresholds values and input data not changed. This underscores the core advantage of simulated quantisation, allowing the creation of a model that is both accurate and efficient.

Conditional operations are the main core of the decision tree structure. Unlike DNN weights and biases, threshold values are associated with the input numerical ranges, typically falling between the numerical ranges of two features. In tubular data, the input features have different distributions, resulting in larger numerical threshold values which dominate the quantisation range of the GBDT model and thus minimise features with smaller numerical ranges. In GBDT, similar approaches such as tree-wise quantisation can be applied, but will increase resource usage where each tree requires at least one multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation per tree level. For some type of GBDT models, the number of threshold values per tree is not large enough compared to DNN weights, making the quantisation process impractical. For a symmetrical GBDT tree with a depth of 3, for example, only 3 numerical unique threshold values will be allowed per tree, allowing the largest and smallest values to be quantised, but not the middle one.

It is crucial, therefore, to standardise datasets with unbalanced feature numerical ranges as this will enable the training of the quantised GBDT model using a single scale and zero-point values for thresholds and leaf values whilst maintaining high accuracy. Fig. 3 illustrates the decision boundaries of the GBDT model when trained on the test example from the wine dataset [42] with original and standardised features. The test dataset comprises two features with different numerical distributions and three classes. It was used for training the GBDT model with 10 trees and a depth of 3; it was first quantised to a 4-bit integer and then dequantised. Evaluation on both original and standardised data shows that the quantisation effect significantly influences the model’s decision boundaries for the original dataset. Specifically, Fig. 3b shows a discernible increase in misclassification (as indicated by the overlapping regions) when the model is trained with non-standardised and then quantised, suggesting a loss in the model’s ability to differentiate between classes. After standardisation, however, as shown in Fig. 3d, the GBDT model is able to maintain a similar level of classification accuracy, with the decision boundaries still fitting well within the distribution of the two features. When combined with QAT of GBDT, it ensures that any quantisation error produced is minimal and that all feature values are distributed around the same numerical range and do not affect learning accuracy. Furthermore, the GBDT model demonstrates enhanced robustness to rounding noise produced by quantisation, as shown by the clear separation of classes in the standardised and quantised decision boundaries.

In our implementation, we applied quantisation-aware training to the CatBoost GBDT framework [7], chosen for its use of oblivious decision trees, also known as decision tables. These are advantageous in the simplicity of having a single threshold per tree level, which aligns well with our quantisation approach. This structure not only facilitates easier quantisation but also results in balanced trees that are less affected by overfitting. The underlying principles of our approach are also applicable across other GBDT frameworks, such as XGBoost [5] and LightGBM [6].

In DNN, it is well known that during training with QAT, the process faces a challenge where the learning loss does not decrease. Thus, it is a usual practice to run several epochs before quantising the model parameters. Similarly, we have noticed that when training the GBDT model with low precision data types, e.g. 4-bits integer, the learning loss will reach a stage where it does not decrease (see Fig. 4a). We observed that if we quantise for every N iterations of tree building, the GBDT model will learn much better and overcome that challenge. However, this will still be considered as a hyper-parameter tuning approach, and increasing the number of iterations may not result in better performance even with higher precision (see Fig. 4b).

section: V. GENERATIVE HARDWARE IMPLEMENTATION OF GBDT
text: The primary consideration for quantised inference is the efficient hardware deployment of ML models. For GBDT, this encompasses various factors related to model training and inference, such as classification tasks and datasets. Two main considerations include: the choice of the hardware device and the model’s transition (exporting) to the chosen device. FPGAs are selected as the implementation device due to their significant capabilities for exploiting the reduced precision and the reconfigurability of their hardware components. Moreover, FPGAs are noted for their parallel computing abilities and fast inference times with lower power consumption compared to CPUs and GPUs (graphics processing units). Additionally, for full on-chip implementation of the GBDT model, the FPGA is regarded as the primary choice for verifying the realization of low-powered System-on-Chip (SoC) devices.

Process to convert binary GBDT trees into FPGA-optimised logic circuits. It comprises the mapping of decision trees, logic minimisation, and final C++ code generation to be exported to the HLS (High-Level Synthesis) tool.

They are particularly suited for realisation of the oblivious trees used by CatBoost. Many GBDT tree implementations have been converted into LUT hardware using the Conifer package [10]. It allows users to export quantised GBDT models into FPGA hardware and select any arbitrary precision against a target operation frequency and specific FPGA device. Conifer package also requires the AMD-Xilinx High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tool, Vitis HLS, and Vivado to realise the implementation. CatBoost and Conifer packages work directly with Python to facilitate an easy and rapid transition to hardware implementations.

subsection: B. Exporting the Binary GBDT Model
text:
Whilst LUTs play a crucial role implementing integer-based GBDT models, binary GBDT models can be even more efficiently mapped to FPGA as they require fewer resources due to their single-bit representation. In contrast to the Conifer-based approach for quantised GBDT models, we have developed a method that significantly reduces the complexity of tree conversion, resulting in a more compact and efficient use of LUTs for binary trees. Our specialised binary tree exportation technique leverages the characteristics of binary decisions to achieve an optimal mapping onto the FPGA’s logic fabric and optimises the conversion process specifically for FPGA implementation. We refer to the compact binary implementation as BinaryGBDT.

The method, described in Fig. 5, begins by mapping each individual binary tree into a truth table, which captures the behavior of the tree across all possible input combinations since input is either 1 or 0. From this truth table, the binary tree is then transformed into Boolean expressions that represent the decision logic of the tree. Subsequently, a twolevel logic minimization [43] is employed to further compress these Boolean functions, leading to a more efficient hardware implementation.

After minimizing the logic, we compile each tree into C++ code, which encapsulates the optimised decision-making process of the binary tree, making it ready for integration into HLS and with Conifer C/C++ files. HLS generates the FPGA implementation and performs more logic minimizing across all

section: V. GENERATIVE HARDWARE IMPLEMENTATION OF GBDT
text: A Python environment is employed to assist with the quantised training of the GBDT model, and the subsequent export to the HLS tool is achieved through integration with the Conifer framework (v1.4). CatBoost is utilised for the training of the GBDT model and is complemented by additional back-end processing stages from our approach, which introduces quantisation during training, as described in Section IV. Users are required to specify a range of parameters including the number and depth of trees, learning rate, data type and wordlength, as well as the type of quantisation (signedsymmetric, or signed-asymmetric), the number of iterations to wait-then quantise, and the dataset. Following training, Conifer exports the quantised CatBoost model as an .onnx file to C++/C code in AMD-Vitis 2023.1 for synthesis. The target clock speed is set to 500 MHz to facilitate resource utilisation and the export of the IP core’s RTL designs. Vivado 2023.1 is utilised for placement and routing. The Vivado tool may optimise the model to achieve a maximum operational frequency (Fmax), surpassing the targeted frequency, as shown in Table II, which is presented in the next section. To prevent overflow in all scenarios, the ensemble sum is constrained to a 32-bit signed integer. The FPGA platform used is the AMD-Xilinx Kria KV260 AI board, and designs are implemented on its Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC FPGA, comprising 147,720 LUTs, 234,240 flip-flops (FFs), 1,248 digital signal processing (DSP) slices, 144 block RAMs (BRAMs), and 64 Ultra-RAMs (URAMs).

section: V. GENERATIVE HARDWARE IMPLEMENTATION OF GBDT
text:
The performance of our quantised GBDT model is evaluated using datasets that are pivotal for applications in high-energy physics and cybersecurity to demonstrate the model’s efficacy across various domains necessitating ultra-low latency and high accuracy.

1) Network Intrusion Detection (NID): In the realm of cybersecurity, the network intrusion detection application utilises the UNSW-NB15 dataset [18], which comprises network packets labelled as either normal or malicious, with 49 features extracted from simulated modern intrusion attacks. This dataset enables us to assess our quantised GBDT model’s proficiency in high-performance packet processing systems, particularly those implemented on FPGAs, offering a balance between speed and programmability. Additionally, a binarised version of the dataset is obtained by following the preprocessing and feature conversion approach outlined by [32]. Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in the real-time detection of malicious activities at the edge of the network, ensuring security without introducing throughput bottlenecks.

2) Jet Substructure Classification (JSC): The Jet Substructure Classification (JSC) task plays a crucial role in analysing data from large-scale physics experiments, such as those conducted at CERN. Specifically, this task is applied to the FPGA-based triggers of the ATLAS and CMS experiments, which are required to process data at a rate of 40 MHz whilst maintaining a µs response latency. This multi-classification task, utilising a 16-input and 5-output model as formulated by [44], showcases our quantised GBDT model’s capacity to manage the high-throughput data processing demands. The JSC dataset [19] serves as a benchmark for evaluating the model’s performance in a domain where precision and speed are paramount for edge computing applications [10], [32], [35], [44]. While this work provides FPGA implementations for this task, our focus is on demonstrating how our quantised GBDT model compares in terms of efficiency and applicability.

This section outlines the outcomes from evaluating the quantisation-aware training of GBDT models with different configurations listed in Table I. The choice of settings reflects the principles discussed in the Modeling Environment section, (Section V-C). Also, comparisons with state-of-art FPGA implementations are discussed, reflecting the efficiency of the proposed approach on popular benchmarks.

A. AUC Over Reduced Precision: PTQ Vs. QAT

The efficacy of QAT over PTQ is empirically validated in Fig. 6, which depicts AUC metrics for GBDT models subjected to varying levels of quantisation precision. Here, the AUC values are used to indicate the model performance based on dropped accuracy compared to the floating-point reference model. The results for the binary classification case (Fig. 6a) reveal that QAT outperforms PTQ consistently. Even at reduced bit-widths, QAT maintains AUC levels close to those achieved with higher precision, showcasing its effectiveness in learning quantisation-resilient features. In multiclass classification case (Fig. 6b), a similar pattern is observed.

subsection: C. Accuracy Over FPGA Resource Utilisation
text:
There is a discernible trade-off, as reduced LUT utilisation often accompanies a decrease in accuracy, presenting key challenges in compressed design. In the binary classification task, as depicted in Fig. 8a, a noticeable improvement in model accuracy is observed as LUT utilisation increases from 1-bit to 16-bit precision models. The GBDT-int16 model achieves the highest accuracy, which also requires the most LUTs, underscoring that higher computational resource use enhances accuracy. For the multiclass classification task (JSC dataset), illustrated in Fig. 8b, enhanced precision and associated LUT utilisation similarly improve accuracy. However, the increase in accuracy from GBDT-int8 to GBDT-int16 is less significant compared to the binary classification, indicating that additional LUT usage results in diminishing returns on accuracy at higher precision levels. The BinaryGBDT model exhibits lower LUT utilisation compared to the binary model in both tasks, highlighting that greater precision, while beneficial, demands more FPGA resources, often without proportional gains in accuracy.

D. RTL-Synthesis Comparisons With Prior Work

This analysis explores the efficiency and performance enhancements delivered by the Quantised GBDT (QGBDT) and BinaryGBDT models across the NID and JSC benchmarks. The focus is to show the advantages of these models in

terms of accuracy, resource utilisation (LUTs, FFs), and operational frequency (Fmax), underscoring the significant improvements over existing methodologies. The RTL-synthesis results discussed next are presented in Table III and reported numbers are from their referenced work.

1) NID Task Insights: On the NID task, the BinaryGBDT model demonstrates a notable achievement by maintaining a high accuracy (92%) while utilising dramatically fewer resources – a remarkable 4.7x and 5.4x reduction in LUTs compared to the LogicNets and Murovic et al. models, respectively. Furthermore, the BinaryGBDT model showcases an unparalleled operational frequency, Fmax, standing at 1013 MHz, which is over 2.15x higher than that achieved by the PolyLUT (NID Lite) model. This unprecedented efficiency not only speaks to the model’s computational prowess but also its potential for real-time applications requiring high-speed processing.

The GBDT-int8 model further proved the capability of QGBDT models, achieving the same accuracy (92%) as the BinaryGBDT but with a slight increase in resource demands. Nevertheless, its operational frequency impressively exceeds that of traditional BNN approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of GBDT quantisation in achieving a balance between accuracy and high-speed performance.

2) JSC Task Insights: For the JSC task, both the BinaryGBDT and QGBDT models again set new benchmarks. The BinaryGBDT model, with its 73.5% accuracy, not only surpasses the performance of competing methods like LogicNets and NullaNet Tiny in accuracy but does so with significantly lower resource consumption. Specifically, it achieves a 3.05x reduction in LUT count compared to the LogicNets (JSC-L) model and boasts an Fmax that is nearly 2x higher, emphasising its superior efficiency and speed.

The GBDT-int8 model has a compelling advantage by offering the best accuracy (75%) among the GBDT configurations. It achieves this with an Fmax of 1028 MHz, highlighting a significant improvement in operational speed compared to GBDT fixed-point implementations by Summer et al. [10]. It is appreciated that 1 GHz running frequency will not be achievable in most conventional FPGA hardware platforms, but the aim is to give raw performance figures for comparison. This model exemplifies the strength of quantisation in enhancing model performance without compromising on speed, even in multi classification tasks.

For FPGA RTL-implementation results produced after place and route with an initiation interval (II) of 1, the QGBDT models exhibit remarkable performance over existing methodologies. To ensure a fair comparison, the projects were compiled under similar settings used in LogicNets studies, specifically using the Flow_PerfOptimized_high configurations and performing synthesis in the Out-of-Context (OOC) mode. In terms of power efficiency, both the BinaryGBDT and GBDT-int8 models demonstrate significant advancements over other approaches across the two tasks. For the NID task, BinaryGBDT exhibits exceptionally low dynamic power consumption at only 17 mW, which is considerably lower than that of the LogicNets model, consuming 95 mW. Similarly, in the JSC task, BinaryGBDT maintains its superior power efficiency with a dynamic power consumption of 69 mW, compared to the significantly higher 1300 mW by the LogicNets (JSC-L) implementation. The GBDT-int8 model also outperforms the LogicNets in JSC tasks, consuming 159 mW and 506 mW in the NID and JSC tasks respectively.

Gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT) offer the potential to provide hardware efficient implementations due to their use of less complex logic. In this paper, we explore quantisation techniques commonly used for DNN implementations, namely the post-training quantisation (PTQ) and quantisation-aware training techniques (QAT). We identify that combining QAT with GBDT ensures that any quantisation error produced is minimal and that all feature values are distributed around the same numerical range and do not affect learning accuracy. A framework was then developed permitting a range of GBDT designs to be produced, which offer superior performance over existing research. In case of embedded-AI, the performance of any embedded solution will be limited by training on limited dataset and simpler models and will not provide the performance of cloud-based solutions, which have been trained on large datasets with very large complex models. Thus, future work will be to explore how the system could be incorporated in a cloud/embedded solution. In addition, the work is part of a larger project involved in developing an
